answers: A man convicted four years ago in the oldest cold case ever tried was freed Friday after an Illinois judge vacated his conviction and subsequent life sentence, CNN reports. According to CBS News, 76-year-old Jack McCullough was convicted of kidnapping a 7-year-old girl, choking her, and stabbing her to death in 1957. The case was reopened in 2008, and McCullough was arrested in 2011 and convicted the following year. After an appeal by McCullough, Illinois state's attorney Richard Schmack launched a six-month investigation that found what he calls "clear and convincing evidence" that McCullough is innocent. While the judge Friday vacated McCullough's conviction, he stopped short of declaring him innocent, and a new trial will be held, the Chicago Tribune reports. McCullough, who lived in the same neighborhood as the kidnapped girl, says he was 40 miles away at an Air Force recruiting center at the time of the kidnapping. It's an alibi that passed a polygraph test in 1957 and made it impossible for him to be the culprit based on the FBI's original timeline for the kidnapping. That timeline was later changed by police, and Schmack says documents—including phone and Air Force records—supporting McCullough's alibi were wrongly not allowed at his trial. A friend of the kidnapped girl picked McCullough out of a photo lineup when the case was reopened. But his was the only non-yearbook photo in the lineup, and she picked a different man out of a photo lineup 50 years earlier. That info wasn't allowed at McCullough's trial either. No physical evidence was ever found to support McCullough's conviction.

In a landmark ruling, a 76-year-old man, Jack McCullough, who was convicted in 2012 of the 1957 murder of 7-year-old Maria Ridulph, has been ordered released from prison and granted a new trial. The decision was made by Judge William Brady in Sycamore, Illinois, following a comprehensive review of the case by DeKalb County State's Attorney Richard Schmack. McCullough, who has long maintained his innocence, was found to have been 40 miles away in Rockford, Illinois, at the time of the abduction, based on newly discovered phone records that confirmed his alibi.

Maria Ridulph was abducted while playing in the snow with a friend on December 3, 1957. A man approached the children, introduced himself as "Johnny," and took Maria for a piggyback ride. Maria's friend returned home to get mittens and found her and the man missing. The case went unsolved for over 50 years until a tip from McCullough's half-sister, Janet Tessier, led to his arrest in 2011. Despite a polygraph test that cleared him, McCullough was convicted in a trial that many questioned for its one-sided nature.

Schmack, who took over the case after the original prosecutor, Clay Campbell, found new evidence that supported McCullough's alibi. He reviewed over 4,500 pages of documents, including old police reports, FBI files, and even a CNN series on the case, which raised doubts about the original trial. Schmack concluded that there was "clear and convincing evidence" that McCullough was wrongfully convicted.

McCullough's conviction was upheld by an Illinois appeals court in 2022, but he continued to appeal, arguing that evidence supporting his alibi was buried. Schmack's review led to the judge's decision to overturn the conviction. McCullough, who was released shortly after the ruling, was seen smiling at his stepdaughter, signaling his affection, while Maria's family, particularly her brother Charles Ridulph, expressed disappointment and disbelief.
